extracted.intended_audience: investors, financial journalists, regulators, and analysts following corporate governance and market-manipulation risks
extracted.subtask_description: An investigative financial report identifying indicators of stock parking, opaque offshore fund structures, and possible market manipulation tied to a corporate group. Uses shareholding disclosures, delivery-volume metrics, corporate records, and interviews to assess whether public investors are actually promoter-controlled entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of beneficial ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Adani Group secretly controls significant amounts of publicly traded stock without disclosure, the resultant share price of Adani listed companies could be easily manipulated to meet the immediate needs of the Adani Group (i.e., to give the appearance of liquidity, to help raise money, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs) of funds holding company stock are disclosed; undisclosed promoter control of so-called public shares is a red flag for manipulation and misclassification of insider holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum public shareholding / non-promoter public float requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian regulations require listed companies to maintain a non-promoter public float of at least 25%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate promoter vs non-promoter holdings relative to the 25% public-float threshold; companies above the promoter-ownership threshold risk delisting (examples: Adani Enterprises, Adani Transmission, Adani Power, Adani Total Gas, Adani Wilmar).

rubrics_metrics.name: FPI >1% reporting threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Shareholding lists in India only specifically name foreign funds (FPIs) if they hold more than 1% of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sub-1% foreign holdings as potentially opaque vehicles; investigators should aggregate below-threshold holders when assessing promoter control because small unnamed FPIs can be used to conceal ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund transparency and public presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Major holders of large public equities generally share basic characteristics: well-known investment funds with websites that share essential details such as key employees and contact information; basic information like history and source of funds; marketing documents and clear fundraising sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use absence of a public web presence, lack of identifiable employees, missing marketing materials, or no press/news coverage as indicators that a named 'fund' may be a shell or nominee vehicle rather than an independent institutional investor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund diversification and trading behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate funds generally have numerous investments as part of a diversified portfolio; in contrast, many named Adani 'public' funds have little to no diversification and simply hold shares in Adani listed companies for long periods and appear price insensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag funds whose portfolios are narrowly concentrated in a single group's stocks or that show price-insensitive, long-term holding of volatile positions as suspicious and possibly promoter-controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common corporate attributes across funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups of supposedly independent funds formed out of the same jurisdiction by the same incorporator, from the same address, and with overlapping nominee directors indicate relatedness and possible common control (example: five Mauritius funds formed by the same incorporator/address with overlapping nominee directors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify shared incorporators, registered addresses, nominee directors, or LEI linkages across multiple funds as evidence they may be controlled by the same promoter rather than independent investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of holdings across related funds
rubrics_metrics.description: A small group of related funds collectively holding very large positions in a set of listed companies is inconsistent with normal investor behaviour and suggests coordinated ownership (example: Monterosa-related funds collectively holding INR 360 billion in Adani listed companies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate holdings across related entities when evaluating exposure; unusually large aggregated positions concentrated in a related set of companies should be treated as potential promoter parking rather than independent investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close ties between funds and promoters/regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims or evidence that a fund or its operators are 'very close' to government or regulatory officials (or to the corporate group's promoters) suggest corrupt alignment and risk of regulatory capture (quotes alleging SEBI 'working hand in glove').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate personal, corporate, or historic ties between fund operators and promoter/regulatory officials; such ties heighten the risk that reported ownership and trading patterns are being permitted or overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related-party transactions linking funds to corporate group
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a corporate-group related party invested money in a suspect offshore fund (example: Gudami International invested in Lotus Global Investments) constitutes a direct linkage between the group and the purportedly independent fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search disclosures, annual reports, and related-party notes for investments, shared directors, or shareholder overlaps tying offshore funds to the corporate group; such links support classification of the fund as promoter/insider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme portfolio concentration (fund holding ~99% in one group's stocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funds that are almost exclusively invested in one group's stocks (example: Elara India Opportunities Fund 98.78% invested in three Adani stocks) are functionally not independent funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat funds with extremely concentrated positions (e.g., >90% in a single group's securities) as highly suspicious and likely controlled by the issuer/promoter; do not assume they provide independent public float.

rubrics_metrics.name: P-note / SMA structures masquerading as funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehicles structured as separately managed accounts or participatory-note-like arrangements that buy specific shares on instruction may masquerade as funds but function as nominee accounts (quoted: 'It’s a P-note structure masquerading as a fund').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a fund is a pooled vehicle or an SMA/P-note-like arrangement; SMAs or instructable accounts that buy bespoke positions for a single beneficial owner should be treated as nominee vehicles rather than independent investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections to known market manipulators or fugitives
rubrics_metrics.description: Management or directors of funds who have past business dealings with known market manipulators or fugitives (example: Elara’s CEO dealing with Dharmesh Doshi) raise concerns about the fund’s independence and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check executives' histories and email/leak records for ties to previously sanctioned/manipulative actors; such associations are strong indicators of potential abuse or collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corporate services firms with laundering history
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on corporate-services providers with documented roles in past money-laundering or sham-fund schemes (example: Amicorp's ties to 1MDB) signals elevated risk that funds are facades for hiding beneficial owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the corporate-services providers (incorporators, nominee directors, administrators) used by suspect funds; a provider’s prior involvement in laundering or sham structures heightens suspicion of current entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous incorporation patterns indicating control
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity formed on the exact same day, in the exact same jurisdiction, by the same registered agent as another entity tied to a promoter suggests coordinated creation and likely common control (example: Opal and Krunal formed same day by Trustlink).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for coincident incorporations (dates, registrar, agent) among entities linked to a promoter; such patterns are evidence of deliberate structuring to conceal ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: High delivery-volume share by suspect entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspected stock-parking entities accounting for a very large share of delivered volume (e.g., 30%-47% for certain Adani stocks in some years) is anomalous and suggests artificial inflation of volume/price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use percentage of delivery volume attributable to suspect offshore/related entities as a metric; unusually high proportions indicate potential cornering or coordinated trading that can distort prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of delivery volume as detection metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery volume is a unique daily data point provided by Indian exchanges that captures large institutional flows and excludes day-trading activity; it can be used to analyze trading among FPIs and detect suspicious patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ delivery-volume analysis (as opposed to total volume) to track institutional trading flows and identify disproportionate activity by particular FPIs or related groups across time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronized trading among suspect entities across years
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns where the same set of suspect entities repeatedly account for large portions of delivery volume in a stock across multiple years suggests coordinated trading rather than independent investment (detailed per-stock year-by-year percentages provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare top-holder disclosures and delivery-volume contributions across multiple years to identify repeated, synchronized trading patterns among the same offshore entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchases timed to meet minimum public shareholding requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In Q2 2019 several suspected stock-parking entities purchased just enough stock in Adani Green Energy to avoid violation of minimum public shareholding rules, suggesting purchases were intended to create the illusion of independent public float.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine timing and amounts of purchases relative to regulatory thresholds (e.g., 25% public float) and offerings; abrupt purchases that coincide with regulatory needs may indicate orchestrated transactions rather than genuine public demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compromised or connected brokers as bookrunners
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting small, potentially compromised brokers with histories of market-rigging (example: Monarch Networth Capital) or where the group has an interest in the broker raises the risk that offerings were managed to advantage the promoter and its nominee buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review bookrunners' regulatory histories and ownership links to the issuing group; use of brokers with prior manipulation sanctions or group ties is a red flag for engineered sales and distribution to related entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before-and-after holdings changes to infer offering participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial increases in suspect entities' stakes between pre-offer and post-offer public disclosures (example: increases of 6.85%-11.8% during Adani Green Energy offerings) strongly suggest those entities bought into the offering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare disclosed top-holder positions immediately before and after offerings to infer which entities participated; sudden, coordinated stake increases by suspect offshore funds indicate related-party participation in the sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of holdings (promoter vs public) affects listing status
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper classification of a holding as an insider/promoter rather than a public investor can change whether a company meets minimum public-float rules, potentially resulting in delisting (example: reclassifying even one holding could have caused Adani Green Energy to fail the 25% threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether holdings should legally be classified as promoter/related-party rather than public; reclassification can have material regulatory and listing consequences, so scrutinize beneficial-ownership links carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical regulatory findings and settlements as evidence of pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: SEBI and parliamentary inquiries have in the past investigated and sanctioned promoters and other entities for past stock manipulation (example: Ketan Parekh scam 1999–2001 and subsequent SEBI rulings implicating Adani promoters), indicating a historical pattern of alleged market abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use past regulatory findings, bans, and settlements as supporting evidence when evaluating current allegations; a documented historical pattern of manipulation strengthens the case that current opaque structures and trading patterns are part of a recurring strategy.
